I am interested in developing more theorems around elliptic functions (starting with https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Elliptic/Weierstrass.html). I'd like to know its current status: is it already being worked on, or is it reasonable for me to try working on it?

Let me start with asking about a basic theorem that I find missing: every elliptic function is a rational combination of ℘ and ℘'. What would be the best way to state "rational combination"? On the paper, this is often thought in the field of meromorphic functions, but meromorphic functions in Mathlib, as far as I know, is a bit awkward due to junk values at poles. Is Mathlib's infrastructure ready to state this theorem, or something around meromorphic functions need to be developed first?

Weiyi Wang said:

What would be the best way to state "rational combination"?

Maybe ∈ Set.range (Finsupp.linearCombination ℚ ![℘, ℘']) if you want to be fancy, but probably a simple ∃ a b : ℚ, ... is best.
(idk the maths here; I'm assuming "rational combination" means a linear combination with rationals but maybe not)
It is not just linear combination with rationals. 1/℘ is also valid

Snir Broshi said:

(idk the maths here; I'm assuming "rational combination" means a linear combination with rationals but maybe not)

I'm guessing it means the subfield generated by the ℘ and ℘' and ℂ
Yeah, equivalent way to write this is that the field of elliptic functions = ℂ(℘, ℘')

But I don't think the LHS "field of elliptic functions" (= subfield of meromorphic functions with double period) is statable yet, as we don't have field of meromorhic functions yet (?). To develop that one needs to work with docs#MeromorphicNFAt and patch all the junk values.
So I guess my question is, should this wait for the full development of field of meromorphic functions, or is there a elementary statement we can go for first?

Aaron Liu said:

I'm guessing it means the subfield generated by the ℘ and ℘' and ℂ

So maybe ∈ IntermediateField.adjoin (F := ℂ) {℘, ℘'}? (docs#IntermediateField.adjoin)
An intermediate (sub)field of what big field? That's the question.
I don't think we have the field of meromorphic functions (docs#Meromorphic functions modulo docs#Filter.EventuallyEq on docs#Filter.codiscrete) in mathlib yet

Note that things are delicate here: if a meromorphic function has junk values at its poles then things like sum of meromorphic functions cannot be computed naively: if e.g. (1/z) has junk value 0 at z=0 and ((z-1)/z) also has junk value zero at z=0 (and these are the values which Lean would assign to them) then their sum will have junk value 0 at 0, but their sum should be the constant function 1. As Aaron says we need need to carefully consider equivalence classes, this is the real problem here. Note that Weierstrass P and its derivative both have poles at 0 so this is not just a theoretical problem.
Indeed. Is the recommendation to develop the field of meromorphic functions and handle this part first? Is this being actively worked on?

and (this is going a bit offtopic) if one makes a field of meromorphic functions, should the element be

  • from quotient of MeromorhicOn functions by relation =ᶠ[codiscreteWithin U], or
  • MeromorphicNFOn functions with redefined arithmetic, e.g. f + g is not naive pointwise addition around the pole

Weiyi Wang said:

  • MeromorphicNFOn functions with redefined arithmetic, e.g. f + g is not naive pointwise addition around the pole

Maybe for a meromorphic function f, its evaluation at x is not simply f.toFun x, but the limit of f.toFun y as y tends to x. Since outside the poles f.toFun is continuous, it gives the correct result (even correct for your above f + g, since if the pole cancels out, the limit gives correct answer). If x is a pole of f, then it should give junk value zero (?).
Pinging @Stefan Kebekus on this; I assume he has thought about meromorphic functions a bit.

I'm not sure schemes will answer the original question. We can already make the docs#EllipticCurve associated to a lattice and we have the rational functions on it but by definition it's the field of fractions of C[℘,℘′].\mathbb{C}[\wp,\wp'].C[℘,℘′]. Note that elliptic curves aren't schemes but someone was working on rational maps recently and the issue would be the same. I got my hand dirty with the quotient approach and now I have a Field (MeromorphicOn f U quotient by =ᶠ[Filter.codiscreteWithin U]) for (h1 : ¬ IsDiscrete U) (h1 : U.Nontrivial) (h2 : IsPreconnected U) (Thanks Aristotle for identifying the needed condition). That was a fun exercise and I'll play with it more to see what might be PR-able

One more (unfortunately unsuccessful) idea is to supplement the definition of a meromorphic function by explicitly including its principal (singular) parts at the singular points. Such definition is good for addition/subtraction, multiplication (require regular parts of Laurent series at singular points), and for contour integration around singular points. But it is bad for division: for example, even the definition of 1/f in terms of meromorphic f will need the locations of zeros and the regular parts of f at these locations. Meromorphic functions like 1/P(f), where P is a polynomial, look terrible within such a defintion.

Aside from the meromorphic function equivalent class problem, I think another key missing ingredient is the residue theorem. The classic result of elliptic function is "sum of residue" and "sum of meromorphic order" within a fundamental parallelogram is zero, and on paper this is an instant result by taking the contour integral on the parallelogram. Does mathlib have enough tool to do contour integral like this? (I see rectangle one and circle one, but not a generic one)

I have a generalised residue theorem for piecewise C1 paths, that was proven by Claude (following this) on the way to the Valence formula for modular forms. This should work for what you want, but its still very much in the clean up stage.

I have (=Claude Fable has) meanwhile produced a first implementation of the "field of meromorphic functions", and I would like to welcome your feedback.

Main points:

  • There are two distinct objects: Meromorphic functions as we already have them, and germs of meromorphic modulo the codiscrete filter. The second has the structure of a field.
  • The API remarks that meromorphic functions form a ring. Mathlib then knows that the quotient inherits a ring structure and that the quotient map is a ring morphism.
  • If the domain is connected, then germs are invertible and --voilá-- we have an instance of a field.

Find my implementation in ProjectVD more precisely in this directory. Naming is still tentative.

@Weiyi Wang I believe meromorphic functions should be defined as sections of meromorphic sheaf on a ringed space. A short introduction is:

Given a topological space X, a presheaf of commutative rings on X is a functor F from the opposite category of the category of open subsets of X to the category of commutative rings, e.g. the collection of holomorphic functions on open subsets of the complex plane form a presheaf.

If the presheaf has a better property (i.e. it can be determined locally), it is a sheaf, e.g. a complex valued function on an open subset of complex plane is holomorphic iff it is holomorphic around every point in that open subset. A topological space together with a chosen sheaf of commutative rings is called a ringed space, and it is already in mathlib.

Given a topological space and a presheaf of commutative rings on it, we can form an associated total quotient presheaf by doing some sort of quotient, and it is done in mathlib by totalQuotientPresheaf : X.Presheaf CommRingCat.{w}. We may also call it the associated meromorphic presheaf. Then after sheafification (a process of getting a canonical sheaf associated to a presheaf), we may call it the associated meromorphic sheaf.

Then with suitable conditions, we may show that the global section of a meromorphic sheaf on a ringed space (i.e. a topological space with a chosen sheaf of commutative rings) is a field. Then we can show that the complex plane together with the sheaf of holomorphic functions, satisfies these conditions.

I believe this should be the correct and general approach. For references, Stacks Project should be helpful, in particular, tag 01X1. It is not elementary, but it is general and, in my opinion, worth implementing. Actually I will do a quick coding to get a minimal theorem around that.

I have done it. See MeromorphicFunction. Feel free to use it, AI did most of the work. The following theorem works for both meromorphic functions on the complex plane and function fields on integral schemes, so it is a unified theorem. @Kevin Buzzard You might find it interesting.

There are three files, the file basic.lean contains the following main theorem:

theorem isField_meromorphicGlobalSections_of_uniqueContinuation (X : LocallyRingedSpace)
    [ConnectedSpace X] [LocallyConnectedSpace X] [HasDomainStalks X] [UniqueContinuation X] :
    IsField X.meromorphicGlobalSections

where HasDomainStalks X means the stalks at every point is a domain and UniqueContinuation X is

class UniqueContinuation (X : LocallyRingedSpace) : Prop where
  eq_of_germ_eq :
    ∀ {U : TopologicalSpace.Opens X} (_hU : IsPreconnected (U : Set X))
      (s t : X.presheaf.obj (op U)) {x : X} (hx : x ∈ U),
      X.presheaf.germ U x hx s = X.presheaf.germ U x hx t → s = t

The file ComplexPlane.lean constructs the locally ringed space as the complex plane together with the sheaf of holomorphic functions on it, and then show that it satisfies the conditions of the main theorem and thus has a field of meromorphic functions. It can be generalized to connected Riemann surfaces. But I didn't do that because it will take more codes to construct the corresponding locally ringed space.

The file IntegralScheme.lean shows integral schemes satisfy the conditions of the main theorem and thus has a function field.

I won't PR them in mathlib myself. For me it's just a quick proof of concepts. Feel free to use it.

@Zhenhua Wu I have read your comments, and I think we are talking about two different projects. I totally agree that one should eventually have (meromorphic|analytic|you-name-it) functions as a sheaf, but in order to do that, we first have to get the local theory right.

The project that @Weiyi Wang came up with is exactly this: define a notion of "meromorphic" that one can use as a local model in complex geometry: "germs of meromorphic functions under the 'codiscrete' filter". Once that is done, let's talk about sheaves.

@Stefan Kebekus The sheaves of meromorphic functions on the complex plane (resp. a ringed space) can be directly constructed from first total quotienting the sheaf of holomorphic functions on the complex plane (resp. the structure sheaf on the ringed space) and then take a sheafification. So strictly speaking, one do need the local model, but the sheaf of holomorphic functions on the complex plane will suffice, then sheaf theory can take it from here.

Of course one can work on meromorphic functions on the local model by first using elementary method and obtain equivalent definition and develop certain properties and theories following textbooks. But eventually we will need to show that this elementary definition agrees with the definition generated by the sheaf of holomorphic functions above.

Actually I believe the germs approach inspired the whole sheaf theory (I'm not sure about the history, but clearly complex analysis has a much longer history than sheaf theory). So the germs approach is essentially the same as the approach using sheaf theory, just one being specific to meromorphic functions and another one being general for any ringed space.

@Zhenhua Wu As I wrote earlier, I think we are talking about two different projects, and your comment "I believe the germs approach inspired the whole sheaf theory" might point to the source of the misunderstanding.

With the definitions that we have in mathlib, the prototypical meromorphic function is the discontinuous function "constant one everywhere and zero at the origin" -- this equals the function f(x) = x/x. As a matter of fact, you can take any meromorphic function and modify it at random over a discrete set; the modified function is still meromorphic. This is the definition typically used in complex analysis ("poles" and "resolvable singularities"). Sometimes, however, one would like to talk about the "field of meromorphic functions". However, with the complex-analysis definition that we have in Mathlib, meromorphic functions do not form a field; the function f(x) = x/xis not the constant function one. What is a field is "meromorphic functions modulo modifications on discrete sets", and this is what @Weiyi Wang is planning to implement.

Now for the confusion: In the terminology of Mathlib, the quotient "vector space of meromorphic functions modulo equality on codiscrete sets" is most easily expressed as "germs of meromorphic functions modulo the codiscrete filter". Note that this is totally different from "germs of meromorphic functions modulo the neighbourhood filter". The second is what people consider a "stalk" in sheaf theory. The first has no relation to sheaves, for all I see.
@Stefan Kebekus I see now. But isn't that definition only work for dim 1 case?

@Zhenhua Wu You are right; this definition works only in the one-dimensional case. Note, however, that Mathlib currently defines meromorphic only in the one-dimensional case!

I totally believe that we should also define the attribute "meromorphic " for functions on higher-dimensional spaces, but this has not been done yet [and is out of scope for my current project on Value Distribution Theory]. As soon as we have "meromorphic on higher-dimensional domains", the same approach will hold once we replace the "codiscrete" filter by "coanalytic = complement of analytic set". But before getting there, we need to set up a whole theory of analytic sets and orders of functions along codimension-one subsets.
So maybe it's better to use total fraction ring of holomorphic functions in higher dimensional case?

@Jz Pan I do not think that you can say one definition is better than the other; it depends on your use case (contour integration? transcendence statements?). In practice, we need both definitions and a good API to go from one side to the other.
